meanings.note: Quintessential Levantine 'why?' (literally 'for what thing?': لـ + إيش).

examples.trans: Why were you late today?
I don't know why she got upset.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine adjective for emotional hurt or annoyance (ليش زعلانة؟).

examples.trans: Mariam looks upset today.
Don't leave here upset.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine manner word: ليش بتحكي هيك؟ ('why are you talking like that?'), زي هيك ('like this'), بعد هيك ('after this').

examples.trans: Don't talk to me like that.
That's not what we agreed on.

meanings.note: Indefinite كل يوم means 'every day'; definite اليوم means 'today' (مش بعد اليوم 'not after today').

examples.trans: We see each other every day at school.
Today the weather is very pleasant.

meanings.note: Plural صحبات is the everyday Jordanian word for girlfriends / school friends (صحباتي، صحباتها).

examples.trans: Dina is my closest friend.
I sat with my friends in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Construes with على for lying to or about someone (كذبوا علي، عم بكذبوا عليكي).

examples.trans: I have never lied to you.
The girls are lying to the principal.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun endings: علي (on/about me), عليكي (to you, f.), عليها (to her), علينا (on/for us), عليكم (on you, pl.). Often contracts to عـ before الـ.

examples.trans: Count on me in this matter.
They lied about me in front of the teacher.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine preposition taking nouns (قدام المديرة) or suffixes (قدامهم 'in front of them').

examples.trans: She stood in front of the whole class.
Act normal in front of them.

meanings.note: Refers to Ms. Faten, headmistress of AlRawabi School.

examples.trans: The principal called us to her office.
We spoke with the principal this morning.

meanings.note: Jordanian plural demonstrative for people: هدول البنات ('these/those girls').

examples.trans: Those girls are in our class.
Who are those people standing over there?

meanings.note: Singular بنت, definite البنت, plural بنات / البنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls' = مدرسة الروابي للبنات).

examples.trans: She is a very bright girl.
The girls are standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine pronunciation (daayman) of classical دائماً.

examples.trans: She always comes early.
We always sit here.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'do' or 'make' (بعمل وظيفة 'doing homework', بعملوا مشاكل 'making trouble').

examples.trans: How did you do on the exam?
I didn't do anything wrong.

meanings.note: Plural مشاكل in بعملوا مشاكل ('they cause trouble').

examples.trans: We don't want trouble at school.
The problem was solved quickly.

meanings.note: After a noun, means 'one' (إشي واحد، سؤال واحد، إيد واحدة); with الـ (الواحد) it is the everyday impersonal subject 'a person / one'.

examples.trans: A person has to tell the truth.
I have just one question.

meanings.note: Followed directly by a subjunctive verb: بيقدر يتحمل ('can endure'), بتقدري تاخدي ('you can take').

examples.trans: You can sit here.
I couldn't sleep yesterday.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine counterpart of ظل; before another verb (يضل يتحمل، بتضلك تخططي) it means 'keep on doing'.

examples.trans: I stayed at school until afternoon.
You keep asking the same question.

meanings.note: Covers enduring mistreatment (يتحمل الظلم) and taking responsibility (نتحمل المسؤولية).

examples.text: ما بقدر أتحمل أكتر من هيك.
examples.trans: I can't put up with more than this.
We must take responsibility.

meanings.note: Signature Jordanian/Palestinian word corresponding to formal شيء; definite form الإشي, plural أشياء.

examples.trans: There is something important I want to say.
Nothing happened.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word (pronounced ktiir) used before or after adjectives ('very') and after plural nouns ('many').

examples.trans: The movie was really good.
I have lots of friends at school.

meanings.note: Short, invariable spoken word for 'true / right' (مش صح 'not true', صح 'right!').

examples.trans: What you say is a hundred percent right.
This claim isn't true.

meanings.note: Used with بقلبه for holding hurt and anger inside until reaching a breaking point.

examples.trans: It isn't good to bottle your hurt up inside.
A person holds things in up to a certain point.

meanings.note: Seat of unspoken feelings: يكبت بقلبه ('bottles things up inside one's heart').

examples.trans: I spoke to you from my heart.
She has a very kind heart.

meanings.note: لمرحلة معينة means 'up to a certain point / stage'.

examples.trans: We reached a difficult stage.
High school is a very important stage.

meanings.note: Follows an indefinite noun to mean 'a certain / particular' (لمرحلة معينة 'up to a certain point').

examples.trans: Do you have a specific time we can meet?
Is there a particular reason for your question?

meanings.note: Conversational pivot word acknowledging what was said before moving on or softening an apology.

examples.trans: Alright, what's the plan now?
Okay sorry, don't be upset.

meanings.note: Core Levantine question word for 'what?' (شو صار؟) and casual conversation starter ('So, ...').

examples.trans: What are you doing here?
So, ready to go?

meanings.note: Levantine 'want' built from بد- plus pronoun suffixes: بدي (I want), بدك (you want), بدنا (we want).

examples.trans: What do you want to do now?
I wanted to talk with you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Levantine word for 'now' (contracted from هاد الوقت).

examples.trans: We have to go to class right now.
I feel a bit relieved now.

meanings.note: Placed before a name or title whenever addressing someone directly (يا دينا، يا مس فاتن); natural English usually drops it.

examples.trans: Come here, Mariam.
Thank you very much, Miss.

meanings.note: Standard Levantine future marker placed before a bare subjunctive verb (رح أخلص، ما رح نسكت).

examples.trans: I'm going to tell the truth.
I won't forget this day.

meanings.note: Form II khallas means 'finish something' (نخلصه), while Form I khalas min (أخلص من ظلمهم) means 'be rid of'.

examples.trans: I finished the homework early.
I'm going to put an end to the problem.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun endings مني (from me), منها (of/from her), منكم (of you): تكون من شلتها ('be part of her clique'), بخاف منها ('afraid of her').

examples.trans: I got off the bus.
Which one of you saw what happened?

meanings.note: Central theme word of the show: يتحمل الظلم ('endure unfairness') and ظلمهم ('their mistreatment').

examples.trans: Injustice is hard for a person to bear.
We won't accept unfairness.

meanings.note: Central setting: مدرسة الروابي للبنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls').

examples.trans: The school is close to our house.
I like going to school early.

meanings.note: Form III verb from حساب: رح نحاسبهم ('we will make them answer for what they did').

examples.trans: The principal will hold everyone accountable.
We must hold them accountable for their mistake.

meanings.note: Spoken form of وراء: spatial 'behind' (ماشيين وراها، من ورا 'from behind') and sequential 'one after another' (واحدة ورا الثانية).

examples.trans: I sat at the desk behind you.
They walked into class one after another.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine pronunciation of ثاني (taani); feminine الثانية means 'the other / the next'.

examples.trans: Let's find another place.
I sat in the second row.

meanings.note: Versatile Levantine word meaning 'but' between clauses and 'only / just' inside a clause.
As a focus adverb before a verb, noun, or imperative, بس narrows or softens the statement.

examples.trans: I tried to speak, but she didn't hear me.
I just want one minute.

meanings.note: With possessive endings, -ة becomes -ت-: خطتي ('my plan'), خطتك ('your plan'), خطتنا ('our plan').

examples.trans: We have a clear plan.
What do you think of our plan?

meanings.note: Agrees with its subject: اليوم كان صعب (masc.), الخطة صعبة (fem.).

examples.trans: It was a hard day for us.
The problem isn't very hard.

meanings.note: Softens adjectives, requests, and verbs (صعبة شوي، ارتحت شوي).

examples.trans: Wait for me a bit by the door.
The test was a little hard.

meanings.note: Answers a question negatively ('no') or forms negative commands before a second-person subjunctive verb (لا تصدقوها! 'don't believe her!').

examples.trans: No Miss, that's not true.
Don't worry, everything is fine.

meanings.note: Invariable modal word followed by a subjunctive verb (لازم نتحمل، مش لازم نلفت نظرهم).

examples.trans: We have to go to class now.
We mustn't talk loudly.

meanings.note: Literally 'bring up'; colloquially لازم نربيهم على غلطهم means 'we must teach them a lesson for their wrongdoing'.

examples.trans: My parents raised me to be honest.
We need to teach them a lesson for their mistake.

meanings.note: With possessive suffix غلطهم ('their mistake / wrongdoing').

examples.trans: Everyone learns from their mistake.
She admitted her mistake in the end.

meanings.note: Used alone or at the start of a reply to give warm reassurance or certainty.

examples.trans: Definitely, I'll come with you.
Of course, Miss.

meanings.note: Negates past and b-present verbs (ما إجيت، ما بعرف) and idioms like ما عليكم ('never mind'); after قبل or بدل (قبل ما، بدل ما) it links a verb clause.

examples.trans: I didn't hear the bell.
Come before the school closes.

meanings.note: Used in Jordanian speech with subjunctive forms like أأذيها ('hurt her') and يأذوا ('they hurt').

examples.trans: I didn't mean to hurt you.
They won't hurt anyone.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine indefinite person word; ما حدا means 'nobody'.

examples.trans: Is anyone in the classroom?
Nobody believed me.

meanings.note: Temporal preposition: مش بعد اليوم ('not after today') and بعد هيك ('after this').

examples.trans: We'll see you after class.
I won't stay quiet after today.

meanings.note: High-frequency Jordanian discourse word meaning 'okay, settled!' or 'drop it / enough!'.

examples.trans: Deal, we're agreed.
Enough, be quiet now.

meanings.note: Independent first-person singular pronoun for any gender.

examples.trans: I am a student at the school.
I didn't say anything.

meanings.note: Takes suffixes معي (with me), معك (with you), معها (with her), معنا (with us), معكم (with you all), معهم (with them), and forms مع السلامة! ('Goodbye!').

examples.trans: Come sit with us.
Goodbye, see you tomorrow!

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun, كل means 'every' (كل يوم، كل إشي); with الـ (الكل) it means 'everyone'; with suffixes (كلنا، كلهم، كلها) 'all of us/them/it'.

examples.trans: Everyone knows the story.
We see each other every day.

meanings.note: Used both literally ('walk a step') and figuratively (معكم بكل خطوة 'with you in every step').

examples.trans: I'm with you every step of the way.
Think carefully before any step.

meanings.note: Primary spoken verb for 'see' across the Levant, also used in farewells like أشوفك بكرة! ('See you tomorrow!') and نشوفك! ('See you!').

examples.trans: I saw everything with my own eyes.
See you tomorrow morning!
